Wise
wīz
a. (having wisdom, skilled in right living; rendering Hebrew chakam, Greek sophos)
From the Saxon wis, knowing, from the root of wit, to know. Hebrew chakam is first a word of practical skill — the craftsman of the tabernacle is chakam-hearted — and only then of moral discernment; the Hebrew never separates knowing from doing.

Biblical Definition

Wise in Scripture describes skill in living rightly before God, and it begins not with intelligence but with fear. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; a man may be learned and not wise, and Scripture repeatedly says so. The word's Hebrew background is the workshop: the men who built the tabernacle were wise-hearted, meaning skilled, and biblical wisdom keeps that flavour of competence applied to the actual business of living. A wise man is therefore teachable before he is anything else — “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Proverbs 1:5) — and the fool by contrast is the man who has stopped listening. Scripture also insists that wisdom is granted, not merely acquired: the testimony of the LORD is sure, “making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7), and the holy scriptures “are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). That last phrase sets the boundary of the word's worth: wisdom that does not run to Christ is not finally wisdom at all. Our Lord commends a shrewdness that is never cynical — “be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew 10:16) — discernment about men held together with innocence toward them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Skilled in right living, discerning, taught of God. Biblical wisdom begins in the fear of the LORD, is granted through the Scriptures, and is aimed finally at salvation in Christ.

expand to see more

WISE, a. s as z. [Sax. wis; G. weise.] Properly, having knowledge; hence, having the power of discerning and judging correctly what is right, and of selecting the best means to accomplish it.

2. Discreet and judicious in the use of means; prudent; as, wise as serpents, Matt. 10.

3. Skilful; dexterous; as, the wise-hearted workmen of the tabernacle, Exod. 36.

4. In Scripture, godly; pious; instructed in the way of salvation; as, wise unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3.

5. Sometimes ironically, worldly-wise; as, the wisdom of this world, which God will confound, 1 Cor. 1.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 1:5 — "A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:"

Matthew 10:16 — "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."

2 Timothy 3:15 — "And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus."

Psalm 19:7 — "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple."

Modern Corruption

Wisdom has been reduced to information on one side and to sentiment on the other — either data or a warm feeling about the universe. Scripture makes it skill in living, rooted in the fear of God and ending in Christ.

expand to see more

The academic reduction treats wisdom as accumulated knowledge, which is why an age with unprecedented access to information is so plainly short of wisdom. Scripture separates the two flatly: the wise man is the one who hears and increases learning, meaning he remains correctable, while the fool may know a great deal and be unteachable. The therapeutic reduction runs the other way, making wisdom a matter of inner attunement, listening to oneself, trusting one's instincts — the exact counsel Proverbs spends thirty-one chapters contradicting, since the heart is deceitful above all things.

Both reductions drop the fear of the LORD, which is where the Bible says wisdom starts, and both drop the destination, which is Christ. Paul says God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and that judgment falls on the credentialed and the intuitive alike. The recovery is 2 Timothy 3:15: the Scriptures make a man wise unto salvation, and any wisdom that leaves him unsaved has failed at the only point that finally matters.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chakam is skilled, from a root of craftsmanship applied to conduct; chokmah is the wisdom personified in Proverbs 8. Greek sophos is the wise man and phronimos the prudent, the word behind wise as serpents.

expand to see more

Hebrew chakam (H2450) — wise, skilful; used of the tabernacle craftsmen and of the godly man alike.

Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; personified in Proverbs 8 and fulfilled in Christ.

Hebrew yirath YHWH — the fear of the LORD, named in Proverbs 9:10 as the beginning of wisdom.

Greek sophos (G4680) — wise; used both of God's wisdom and, ironically, of the world's.

Greek phronimos (G5429) — prudent, shrewd; the word in be ye therefore wise as serpents.

Usage

"Of teachableness as the mark of wisdom: a wise man will hear, and will increase learning (Proverbs 1:5)."

"Of shrewdness joined to innocence: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves (Matthew 10:16)."

"Of the Scriptures' saving purpose: able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15)."
